question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.

The Indian team had its back against the wall, but managed to fight back.
option_2: Stuck in a difficult circumstance with no escape
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Stuck in a difficult circumstance with no escape.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "(to have one's) back against the wall" means to be in a very difficult situation from which there is no easy escape; to be cornered and forced to fight or defend oneself. (मुश्किल में फँस जाना / दीवार से पीठ लगना)

◦ Correct usage: The Indian team had its back against the wall, but managed to fight back — i.e. the team was in deep trouble but still recovered.

• The clue "but managed to fight back" shows that the team was in trouble before it recovered, which confirms the sense of being cornered.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "In extreme joy or exhilaration" is the sense of idioms like "on cloud nine" or "over the moon" — not of this idiom.

• Option 3 "Forced to indulge in propaganda" has no connection with the idiom; propaganda relates to spreading biased information.

• Option 4 "Throwing the opposition off guard" means to surprise someone who is unprepared — that is "to catch someone off guard".

NOTE

• Similar idioms of difficulty: "between the devil and the deep blue sea", "in a tight corner", "in hot water", "up against it", "caught between a rock and a hard place".

• Remember: an idiom's meaning is figurative — it can never be worked out from the literal meaning of its individual words.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

This is the first time / I ate such / a tasty cake.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. I ate such.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• After the structure "This is the first/second/last time ...", the verb of the following clause must be in the present perfect tense (has/have + V3), not in the simple past.

◦ Incorrect: This is the first time I ate such a tasty cake.

◦ Correct: This is the first time I have eaten such a tasty cake.

• Hence the erroneous segment is "I ate such".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "This is the first time" (Option 2) is a correct and complete segment.

• "a tasty cake" (Option 4) is correct — the singular countable noun "cake" correctly takes the article "a".

• Option 3 "No error" is wrong because the sentence clearly contains a tense error.

NOTE

• Rule: It is / This is + the first (second, third, only, best) time + present perfect.

◦ It is the only time I have seen him angry.

◦ That was the first time she had travelled alone. (past reference → past perfect)

• Also note the pattern "such a/an + adjective + noun" (such a tasty cake) versus "so + adjective + a/an + noun" (so tasty a cake).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.

A lover of books
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Bibliophile.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Bibliophile" means a person who loves or collects books. (पुस्तक-प्रेमी)

◦ Word roots: Greek biblio- = book + -phile = lover. So biblio + phile = a lover of books.

◦ Example: The old professor was a true bibliophile whose house was full of rare editions.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Philosopher" — a person who studies or is an expert in philosophy (दार्शनिक).

• Option 2 "Librarian" — a person in charge of a library; he/she manages books but is not necessarily a lover of books (पुस्तकालयाध्यक्ष).

• Option 3 "Teacher" — a person who teaches (शिक्षक).

NOTE

• Related "-phile" words often asked in SSC exams: Anglophile (lover of England/English culture), Francophile (lover of France), Cinephile (lover of cinema), Audiophile (lover of high-quality sound), Oenophile (lover of wine).

• Opposite formation "-phobe/-phobia": Bibliophobia (fear/hatred of books), Xenophobia (fear of foreigners), Claustrophobia (fear of closed spaces), Acrophobia (fear of heights).

• Other book-related words: Bibliography (list of books consulted), Bibliomania (obsessive collecting of books).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Tom waited until __________ to start working on his term paper but managed to finish it just in time.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. the eleventh hour.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "at the eleventh hour" means at the last possible moment; just before it is too late. (ऐन मौके पर / अंतिम क्षण में)

◦ Correct: Tom waited until the eleventh hour to start working on his term paper but managed to finish it just in time.

• The phrase "but managed to finish it just in time" is the clue — it shows the work was begun very late.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• "the twelfth hour", "the thirteenth hour" and "the tenth hour" are not idioms in English; only "the eleventh hour" carries the meaning of the very last moment.

• The expression comes from the Biblical parable of the labourers in the vineyard (Matthew 20), where workers hired at the eleventh hour still received full wages.

NOTE

• Similar idioms/phrases: "in the nick of time", "down to the wire", "at the last minute", "by the skin of one's teeth".

• Note the related adjective usage: "an eleventh-hour decision", "eleventh-hour negotiations".

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

Cordial
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Friendly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Cordial" (adjective) means warm and friendly; hearty; sincerely affectionate in manner. (सौहार्दपूर्ण / मैत्रीपूर्ण)

◦ Example: The two Prime Ministers held cordial talks and shared a friendly handshake.

◦ Root: Latin cor / cordis = heart, so "cordial" literally means "from the heart".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Unfriendly" (अमित्रवत) is the exact antonym of cordial — a common trap in SSC synonym questions.

• Option 3 "Brave" means courageous (बहादुर) — unrelated.

• Option 4 "Aromatic" means having a pleasant smell (सुगंधित) — unrelated.

NOTE

• Synonyms of cordial: friendly, genial, affable, amiable, warm, hearty, congenial, gracious.

• Antonyms of cordial: unfriendly, hostile, cold, aloof, frosty, distant.

• Other words from the same Latin root "cor": courage, accord, concord, discord, record.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Bigger fish to fry
option_2: Having something more important to take care of
option_3: Having work more than one’s capacity
option_4: To be similar to one’s parents in some way
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Having something more important to take care of.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "(to have) bigger fish to fry" (also "other fish to fry") means to have more important matters to attend to; to have something more significant to deal with. (अधिक महत्त्वपूर्ण काम होना)

◦ Example: The manager ignored the minor complaint because he had bigger fish to fry before the audit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "To barely get something done" corresponds to idioms such as "by the skin of one's teeth" or "scrape through".

• Option 3 "Having work more than one's capacity" corresponds to "bite off more than one can chew" or "have one's hands full".

• Option 4 "To be similar to one's parents in some way" corresponds to "a chip off the old block" or "the apple doesn't fall far from the tree".

NOTE

• Idioms of priority/importance: "first things first", "put something on the back burner" (postpone a less important task), "the big picture".

• Note the fish-related idioms often asked: "a fish out of water" (uncomfortable in a situation), "a big fish in a small pond", "fishing for compliments", "something fishy" (suspicious).

question:
There is a spelling error in the given sentence. Select the option that contains the INCORRECTLY spelt word.

The hungery goblin scratched the grammar book with a feather.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. hungery.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "hungry" (H-U-N-G-R-Y), not "hungery". (भूखा)

◦ Correct sentence: The hungry goblin scratched the grammar book with a feather.

• Rule: when the suffix "-y" is added to "hunger", the unstressed "e" of the final "-er" is dropped — hunger → hungr + y = hungry.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "scratched" is correctly spelt — scratch + ed.

• Option 3 "feather" is correctly spelt — F-E-A-T-H-E-R.

• Option 4 "grammar" is correctly spelt — note the ending is "-ar", not "-er"; "grammer" is a very common misspelling.

NOTE

• The same e-dropping pattern: anger → angry, hunger → hungry, winter → wintry, enter → entry, disaster → disastrous, monster → monstrous.

• Frequently misspelt SSC words: occasion, accommodation, embarrass, maintenance, privilege, rhythm, separate, definitely, committee, necessary.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The rusty door made a ________ screeching noise.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. harsh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Screeching" means making a loud, high-pitched, unpleasant, grating sound. The adjective that collocates naturally with such a noise is "harsh" (rough, jarring, unpleasant to hear). (कर्कश)

◦ Correct: The rusty door made a harsh screeching noise.

• The word "rusty" is the context clue — rusted hinges produce an unpleasant, grating sound, not a gentle one.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Options 1 "low", 2 "soft" and 4 "smooth" all suggest a quiet or pleasant sound, which contradicts the meaning of "screeching".

• "harsh screeching noise" is a standard collocation; "soft screeching" is self-contradictory.

NOTE

• Useful sound words for SSC: screech (shrill scraping cry), creak (a long low sound of an old hinge), squeak (a short high sound), rustle (leaves/paper), clatter (hard objects), thud (dull heavy sound), murmur (soft continuous sound).

• Collocation practice: harsh criticism/light/voice/reality; smooth surface/ride/transition; soft whisper/music/voice.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The tone of his voice seemed to ______ that he knew more than he was letting on.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. imply.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Imply" means to suggest or indicate something indirectly, without stating it openly. (संकेत करना / अप्रत्यक्ष रूप से जताना)

◦ Correct: The tone of his voice seemed to imply that he knew more than he was letting on.

• The phrase "letting on" (revealing/admitting) shows that the knowledge was not stated directly, so "imply" fits perfectly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Incise" means to cut into a surface; to engrave (चीरा लगाना / उकेरना) — unrelated.

• Option 2 "Intent" is chiefly a noun (purpose/aim) or an adjective (determined) — it cannot follow "to" as a verb here.

• Option 3 "Inculcate" means to instil an idea or habit in someone by persistent instruction (मन में बैठाना) — it needs a taught value, e.g. "inculcate discipline in students".

NOTE

• Distinguish imply vs infer: the speaker/writer implies (hints), while the listener/reader infers (draws a conclusion). This distinction is a favourite SSC question.

• Synonyms of imply: suggest, hint, insinuate, indicate, intimate, connote.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.

Enormous
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Tiny.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Enormous" means very large in size, quantity or extent; huge. (विशाल / बहुत बड़ा)

• Its antonym is "Tiny", which means extremely small. (बहुत छोटा)

◦ Example: An enormous elephant stood beside a tiny mouse.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 4 "Gigantic" (विशालकाय) is a synonym of enormous, not an antonym — the classic trap option.

• Option 2 "Inapposite" means not suitable or apt (अनुपयुक्त) — unrelated to size.

• Option 3 "Irrelevant" means not connected with the matter in hand (असंगत) — unrelated to size.

NOTE

• Synonyms of enormous: huge, immense, colossal, vast, mammoth, gigantic, prodigious, titanic.

• Antonyms of enormous: tiny, minute, microscopic, minuscule, diminutive, petite, negligible.

question:
There is a spelling error in the given sentence. Select the option that contains the INCORRECTLY spelt word.

The questionnaire appeared to be misrably designed.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. misrably.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "miserably" (M-I-S-E-R-A-B-L-Y), not "misrably". (दयनीय ढंग से / बुरी तरह)

◦ Correct sentence: The questionnaire appeared to be miserably designed.

• Formation: miser + able → miserable, and the adverb replaces the final "-le" with "-ly" → miserably.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "designed" is correctly spelt.

• Option 2 "questionnaire" is correctly spelt — remember the double "n" (question + naire).

• Option 4 "appeared" is correctly spelt — double "p", single "r" before "-ed".

NOTE

• Adverbs ending in "-le" drop "le" and take "-ly": miserable → miserably, probable → probably, terrible → terribly, gentle → gently, simple → simply, comfortable → comfortably.

• Other tricky spellings frequently tested: questionnaire, millennium, harass, liaison, occurrence, argument, exaggerate, conscience.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

COVID-19 _________ structural weaknesses in health systems worldwide and negatively impacted individuals, societies, and economies.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. revealed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Revealed" means made known; exposed something that was previously hidden. (उजागर करना / प्रकट करना)

◦ Correct: COVID-19 revealed structural weaknesses in health systems worldwide and negatively impacted individuals, societies, and economies.

• The pandemic exposed existing weaknesses, so "revealed" is the only verb that fits the object "structural weaknesses".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "concealed" means to hide — the exact opposite of the required meaning.

• Option 2 "laid" is incomplete here; it would need "laid bare" to convey the same sense ("laid bare structural weaknesses").

• Option 3 "hit" does not collocate with "weaknesses"; one hits a target or an economy, not a weakness.

NOTE

• Synonyms of reveal: expose, disclose, unveil, divulge, uncover, lay bare, bring to light.

• Antonyms of reveal: conceal, hide, mask, cover up, suppress, camouflage.

• Note the confusables lay/laid/laid (to place something) versus lie/lay/lain (to recline).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

She will handling the baby as tenderly as possible.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. will handle.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A modal auxiliary such as "will" is always followed by the bare infinitive (V1) — the first form of the verb without "to" and without any inflection.

◦ Incorrect: She will handling the baby ...

◦ Correct: She will handle the baby as tenderly as possible.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "wills handle" — modals never take "-s" for the third person singular; "wills" is wrong here.

• Option 2 "shall handles" — again a modal followed by an inflected verb "handles", which is wrong.

• Option 4 "will handled" — a modal cannot be followed by the past participle/past form "handled".

NOTE

• Rule: Modal + V1 (base form) — can go, may come, must write, should study, will handle, would help, might rain.

• The "-ing" form after "will" is possible only in the future continuous: "will be handling". Without "be", "will handling" is ungrammatical.

• Note also the structure "as + adjective/adverb + as possible" — as tenderly as possible, as soon as possible.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

A old woman suddenly laughed, sounding just like an amused hen.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. A old woman.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The indefinite article "a" is used before a word beginning with a consonant sound, while "an" is used before a word beginning with a vowel sound.

• "Old" begins with the vowel sound /əʊ/, so it must take "an".

◦ Incorrect: A old woman suddenly laughed ...

◦ Correct: An old woman suddenly laughed, sounding just like an amused hen.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "suddenly laughed" (Option 4) is correct — the adverb "suddenly" properly modifies the verb "laughed".

• "sounding just" (Option 2) is correct — a participial phrase describing the manner of laughing.

• "like an amused hen" (Option 1) is correct — "like" is a preposition of comparison and "an" is rightly used before the vowel sound in "amused".

NOTE

• The rule depends on sound, not spelling: an hour, an honest man, an MLA, an X-ray BUT a university, a European, a one-rupee coin, a useful book.

• Do not confuse "like" (preposition, followed by a noun) with "as" (conjunction, followed by a clause).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.

Annoy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Gratify.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Annoy" means to irritate, disturb or make someone slightly angry. (चिढ़ाना / परेशान करना)

• "Gratify" means to please or satisfy someone. (संतुष्ट करना / प्रसन्न करना) — this is the correct antonym.

◦ Example: His rude remarks annoyed the guests, but the host's apology gratified them.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "Vex" (सताना) and Option 3 "Irritate" (चिढ़ाना) are synonyms of annoy, not antonyms — classic trap options.

• Option 4 "Thrill" means to cause a sudden feeling of excitement (रोमांचित करना). It is about excitement, not about removing annoyance, so it is not the best antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of annoy: irritate, vex, exasperate, irk, nettle, provoke, pester, rile.

• Antonyms of annoy: gratify, please, delight, soothe, appease, placate, mollify, comfort.

question:
Four words of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains a spelling error.

All life depends on a healthy planet, but the interwoven systems of atmosphere, oceans, watercourses, land, ice cover and biosphere, which form the natural environment, are threatned by human activities.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. threatned.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "threatened" (T-H-R-E-A-T-E-N-E-D), not "threatned". (संकटग्रस्त / खतरे में)

◦ Formation: threat (noun) → threaten (verb) → threatened (past participle). The "e" of "-en" must not be dropped.

◦ Correct: ... which form the natural environment, are threatened by human activities.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "interwoven" is correctly spelt — the past participle of "interweave" (to weave or blend together).

• Option 3 "biosphere" is correctly spelt — the zone of the earth occupied by living organisms.

• Option 4 "watercourses" is correctly spelt — natural or artificial channels through which water flows.

NOTE

• Verbs formed with "-en" keep the "e" before "-ed": threaten → threatened, strengthen → strengthened, frighten → frightened, lengthen → lengthened, heighten → heightened, widen → widened.

• Environment vocabulary useful for SSC: biosphere (life zone), lithosphere (land), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air), ecosystem, biodiversity.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A storm in a teacup
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Much excitement over something trivial.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a storm in a teacup" means a great deal of anger, excitement or fuss about a very unimportant matter. (छोटी-सी बात पर बड़ा हंगामा / राई का पहाड़ बनाना)

◦ Example: The quarrel over the seating arrangement was just a storm in a teacup; it was forgotten by evening.

• The image is of a violent storm confined to something as small as a teacup — great commotion, tiny cause.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "A signal for upcoming storm" would be "the calm before the storm" or "storm clouds gathering".

• Option 3 "Easy money" corresponds to idioms like "money for jam", "a cash cow" or "easy pickings".

• Option 4 "Suffering in silence" corresponds to "grin and bear it" or "suffer in silence".

NOTE

• The American variant is "a tempest in a teapot".

• Related idioms: "make a mountain out of a molehill" (exaggerate a small problem), "much ado about nothing", "blow something out of proportion".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Varun has to ______ his studies for the sake of his ill father.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. sacrifice.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Sacrifice" means to give up something valuable or important for the sake of some other person or aim. (बलिदान करना / त्याग करना)

◦ Correct: Varun has to sacrifice his studies for the sake of his ill father.

• The phrase "for the sake of" is the key clue — it signals giving something up for someone else's benefit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "imitate" means to copy someone's behaviour (नकल करना) — meaningless with "studies ... for the sake of his ill father".

• Option 3 "reverse" means to turn the other way round or to undo (उलटना) — one cannot "reverse" studies.

• Option 4 "applaud" means to praise or clap for someone (सराहना करना) — does not fit the context of hardship.

NOTE

• Synonyms of sacrifice (verb): give up, forgo, surrender, relinquish, renounce, forsake.

• Useful collocations with "sake": for the sake of, for God's sake, for old times' sake, for one's own sake.

• "Sacrifice" is also a noun: "He made a great sacrifice for his family".

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

Vikram is very stronger than I am.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. very stronger.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Very" is used with the positive degree of an adjective, whereas the comparative degree takes intensifiers such as "much, far, a lot, even, still".

◦ Incorrect: Vikram is very stronger than I am.

◦ Correct: Vikram is much stronger than I am. (or simply "stronger than I am")

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "Vikram is" (Option 3) is correct — a proper subject with the correct singular verb.

• "than" (Option 4) is correct — the comparative "stronger" rightly takes "than".

• "I am" (Option 2) is correct — after "than", the subject pronoun with a verb ("than I am") is standard and grammatical.

NOTE

• Rule: very + positive degree (very strong, very tall); much/far/a lot + comparative degree (much stronger, far better, a lot easier).

• Also remember: very modifies the superlative when it means "of all" — "the very best", "the very first".

• Never use double comparatives/superlatives: "more stronger", "most strongest" are always wrong.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

You are always try with jump over the wall.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. trying to jump.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses "are", so the verb must be in the present continuous form: are + V-ing → "are trying".

• The verb "try" is followed by the to-infinitive when it means "attempt": try to jump.

◦ Incorrect: You are always try with jump over the wall.

◦ Correct: You are always trying to jump over the wall.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "trying in jumping" — "try" is never followed by "in + gerund" in this sense.

• Option 2 "try to jump" — leaves "are try", which is grammatically impossible.

• Option 4 "tried with jump" — wrong tense and wrong preposition after "tried".

NOTE

• Note the meaning difference: "try to do" = make an attempt; "try doing" = experiment with a method. ("Try to open the door" vs "Try turning the key the other way".)

• The adverb of frequency "always" with the present continuous usually expresses irritation or a repeated habit: "He is always complaining".

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.

Kasturi went to the garden looking for her mother. Her dog Rex was waiting (1)____ her. Kasturi picked up a stick and threw it. Rex (2)______ the stick and brought it back. Kasturi ran (3)___ the house. Rex chased her. Kasturi ran through the garden and Rex (4)____ her. Mother yelled at both of them. She told them to stay (5)______ of the garden and play somewhere else. Kasturi apologised to her mother. She went for a bike ride while Rex ran next to the bike.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. for.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "wait" takes the preposition "for" when we mention the person or thing awaited: wait for somebody/something.

◦ Correct: Her dog Rex was waiting for her.

• Rex was in the garden awaiting Kasturi, so "waiting for her" is the only natural completion.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "waiting with her" would mean the dog was waiting alongside her — but Kasturi had just arrived, so this contradicts the passage.

• Option 2 "waiting by her" is not idiomatic here; "by" would only indicate physical position (beside).

• Option 3 "waiting to her" is grammatically wrong — "wait" is never followed by "to" + object.

NOTE

• Other common verb + preposition combinations: wait for, look for, listen to, depend on, insist on, believe in, apologise to (a person) for (a thing), congratulate on, comply with.

• Distinguish "wait for" (await someone) from "wait on" (serve someone, as a waiter does).

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.

Kasturi went to the garden looking for her mother. Her dog Rex was waiting (1)____ her. Kasturi picked up a stick and threw it. Rex (2)______ the stick and brought it back. Kasturi ran (3)___ the house. Rex chased her. Kasturi ran through the garden and Rex (4)____ her. Mother yelled at both of them. She told them to stay (5)______ of the garden and play somewhere else. Kasturi apologised to her mother. She went for a bike ride while Rex ran next to the bike.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. chased.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The whole passage is written in the simple past tense ("went", "picked up", "threw", "brought", "yelled"), so the blank also needs a past form.

• Kasturi threw the stick; the dog therefore chased the stick and brought it back — the natural sequence of a game of fetch.

◦ Correct: Rex chased the stick and brought it back.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "chases" is the simple present and breaks the tense consistency of the passage.

• Option 2 "throws" is present tense and also illogical — Kasturi had already thrown the stick.

• Option 3 "threw" is in the past but repeats an action already performed by Kasturi; the dog fetches, it does not throw.

NOTE

• Tense consistency (sequence of tenses) is a favourite SSC cloze-test rule: once a narrative starts in the past, all connected verbs stay in the past unless a universal truth is stated.

• "Chase" = to run after in order to catch (पीछा करना). Forms: chase – chased – chased.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.

Kasturi went to the garden looking for her mother. Her dog Rex was waiting (1)____ her. Kasturi picked up a stick and threw it. Rex (2)______ the stick and brought it back. Kasturi ran (3)___ the house. Rex chased her. Kasturi ran through the garden and Rex (4)____ her. Mother yelled at both of them. She told them to stay (5)______ of the garden and play somewhere else. Kasturi apologised to her mother. She went for a bike ride while Rex ran next to the bike.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. around.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Run around the house" means to run all over / on every side of the house — exactly what the passage describes, as the very next sentences say "Rex chased her" and "Kasturi ran through the garden".

◦ Correct: Kasturi ran around the house.

• "Around" is the standard preposition of movement encircling or covering an area.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "in the house" would mean inside the building, which contradicts the garden setting of the passage.

• Option 3 "round" is chiefly British and would need a different sense of a single circuit; "around" is the more appropriate and standard choice here.

• Option 4 "about the house" suggests aimless movement inside the house and is not idiomatic with "ran" in this context.

NOTE

• Prepositions of movement: across (from one side to the other), through (from end to end within), around (encircling/all over), along (following a line), into (entering), over (above and across).

• Note "run into somebody" = to meet by chance; "run out of" = to exhaust a supply; "run over" = to knock down with a vehicle.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.

Kasturi went to the garden looking for her mother. Her dog Rex was waiting (1)____ her. Kasturi picked up a stick and threw it. Rex (2)______ the stick and brought it back. Kasturi ran (3)___ the house. Rex chased her. Kasturi ran through the garden and Rex (4)____ her. Mother yelled at both of them. She told them to stay (5)______ of the garden and play somewhere else. Kasturi apologised to her mother. She went for a bike ride while Rex ran next to the bike.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. followed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Two requirements must be met: the verb must be in the simple past (to match the narrative) and it must be a transitive verb that can directly take the object "her".

• "Followed" satisfies both: follow + object (follow her) and it is the past form.

◦ Correct: Kasturi ran through the garden and Rex followed her.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "obey" is in the present tense and gives a wrong meaning — the dog was running after her, not obeying her.

• Option 2 "listen" is present tense and intransitive in this sense; it needs "to" — "listen to her".

• Option 4 "came" cannot take a direct object; we say "came after her" or "came to her", not "came her".

NOTE

• Transitive verbs take a direct object without a preposition. Common SSC traps: follow (not follow to), discuss (not discuss about), enter (not enter into a room), marry (not marry with), resemble (not resemble to), attack (not attack on).

• Note the useful synonyms of follow: pursue, chase, trail, shadow, accompany.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.

Kasturi went to the garden looking for her mother. Her dog Rex was waiting (1)____ her. Kasturi picked up a stick and threw it. Rex (2)______ the stick and brought it back. Kasturi ran (3)___ the house. Rex chased her. Kasturi ran through the garden and Rex (4)____ her. Mother yelled at both of them. She told them to stay (5)______ of the garden and play somewhere else. Kasturi apologised to her mother. She went for a bike ride while Rex ran next to the bike.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. out.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed expression is "stay out of (somewhere)", meaning to keep away from a place; not to enter it. (किसी जगह से दूर रहना)

◦ Correct: She told them to stay out of the garden and play somewhere else.

• The very next words "and play somewhere else" confirm that the mother wanted them away from the garden.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "stay of the garden" is not an English construction.

• Option 2 "stay in of the garden" is ungrammatical; "stay in the garden" would also contradict "play somewhere else".

• Option 3 "stay from of the garden" is ungrammatical.

NOTE

• Useful phrasal verbs with "stay": stay out of (avoid/keep away from), stay away from (keep at a distance), stay up (not go to bed), stay behind (remain after others leave), stay put (remain in the same place).

• Similar "out of" expressions: keep out of trouble, run out of time, out of order, out of the question, out of the blue.
